newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - MobileOne's handphone subscribers grow.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - MobileOne's handphone subscribers grow.

text.p: MobileOne (Asia) Pte Ltd (M1), Singapore's second mobile phone operator, said on Thursday its subscribers would have one of the most technologically advanced networks in the world by the end of the year.

Neil Montefiore, M1 chief executive officer, told Reuters in an interview the company had already attracted more than 35,000 subscribers, or almost 10 percent of the Singapore cellular phone market in three weeks of operations.

Singapore's handphone market was deregulated on April, allowing one new competitor, M1, to compete for the first time with the former monopoly telephone company Singapore Telecommunications Ltd in the mobile phone market.
M1 is also one of three new entrants into the domestic pager market, which was also opened up to competition on April 1.
"I don't want to use the word overwhelming, but the response has been way beyond our expectations," Montefiore said.

"In this first three weeks we must be the most successful entrant into any cellular market either initial, or second, or third, or whatever," he said. "The next challenge is to convince people we're worth staying with."

Industry estimates had previously suggested M1 could attract about 8,000 to 10,000 new users per month with an annual churn rate -- customers switching between providers -- of five to eight percent of the market total.

Describing the Singapore telecoms market as "quite vibrant", Montefiore said he expected M1 to achieve a 30 to 50 percent market share before two new cellular licences were awarded in Singapore in 2000.
M1 is a joint venture of Singapore Press Holdings, Keppel Telecom, Britain's Cable & Wireless and Hong Kong Telecommunications.

Montefiore said M1 had invested about Singapore $65 million (US$45.1 million) in the U.S. developed Code Divison Multiple Access (CDMA) technology that uses high frequency transmissions to allow more users on a given bandwidth, helping prevent airwave congestion.
"In parallel to launching our (existing mobile phone) and pager networks, we are building a CDMA network which will be launched by the end of this year," he said.
"What it will deliver is clarity of voice, almost akin to the fixed network, and much more efficient use of spectrum of frequencies," he said.
"In the end that means you can have more people on the network and in the end that means it will be cheaper to operate, although that's some years down the track," he added.
Keeping abreast of the latest developments was vital as competitive pressures were set to increase, Montefiore said.
Research determining the origin of its customer base -- either first time phone buyers or converts from Singapore Telecommunications -- would be ready in May, he said.
About 30 percent of M1's subscribers were not buying handsets from the firm, but they could be new subscribers buying from hardware suppliers rather than direct from M1, he said.
Montefiore said M1's pager services had got off to a good, if less spectacular start, with about 5,000 subscribers singing up in three weeks
"That's just above our expectations," he said.
